source.title: Model Tampering Attacks Enable More Rigorous Evaluations of LLM Capabilities
source.authors: Zora Che; Stephen Casper; Robert Kirk; Anirudh Satheesh; Stewart Slocum; Lev McKinney; Rohit Gandikota; Aidan Ewart; Domenic Rosati; Zichu Wu; Zi-Kui Cai; Bilal Chughtai; Yarin Gal; Furong Huang; Dylan Hadfield-Menell

page_placements.theme: Comparing attacks and methods: fine-tuning bounds other attacks; unlearning no more robust than safety training
Recovery by internal perturbations other than direction ablation

record.tranche_reason: The study directly tests whether attacks can restore behavior suppressed by unlearning, using WMDP-Bio and a new suite of input-space and model-tampering attacks. It uses established unlearning methods but does not reproduce the original studies’ recovery experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper reports WMDP-Bio results for the best checkpoint from each unlearning method and aggregate fine-tuning findings. It also reports latent- and embedding-space attack results in figures, but the text does not give separable numerical outcomes for those attacks. The many-shot and translation attack outcomes are stated explicitly. The separate refusal/jailbreaking experiments concern compliance with harmful requests, not recovery of unlearned biology knowledge. No direction-ablation experiment, quantization attack, or analysis showing that unlearning blocks access rather than deletes knowledge is reported.
record.test_reason: The authors unlearn WMDP-Bio from Llama-3-8B-Instruct with 8 methods, including RMU (the WMDP original's method), TAR, RepNoise and RMU+LAT. They then measure how much WMDP-Bio accuracy comes back under 5 input-space attacks (GCG, AutoPrompt, BEAST, PAIR, a human prompt) and 6 model-tampering attacks (embedding and latent perturbation, WandA pruning, benign, LoRA and full fine-tuning). Many-shot and translation attacks are reported only in words. These results bear directly on A, B, E and F. The study is not one of the original sources.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that no unlearning method resists all attacks and that state-of-the-art unlearning is reversed within 16 fine-tuning steps, sometimes one (Table 4 lists some attacks with more steps and examples). TAR resisted fine-tuning, but only with poor utility, which the authors call unremarkable. They also conclude that model-tampering attacks, especially fine-tuning, predict and conservatively bound the success of held-out input-space attacks, and that robustness lies on a low-dimensional subspace. They argue tampering-based evaluations should complement input-space ones, while noting that tampering success on WMDP-Bio did not predict a separate UK AISI bio evaluation well.
record.recipe_differences: The study implements established unlearning methods, including RMU, on Llama-3-8B-Instruct with WMDP-Bio, then evaluates them with a new suite of input-space and model-tampering attacks. It selects each method’s checkpoint with the highest unlearning score for the headline comparison.
record.method_sensitivity: Recovery varied by unlearning method and attack type. The paper reports weaker fine-tuning recovery for TAR, whose general utility was poor; one-step recovery exceeded 25 percentage points for 6 of 8 implemented methods. Input-space and model-tampering attack results also differed.

fits_no_version.finding: Latent-layer (layer 5) and embedding-space ℓ2-bounded perturbation attacks raise WMDP-Bio accuracy. The latent attack beats 72% of input-space attacks (average relative strength 2.94) and the embedding attack beats 54% (0.99). Both correlate with input-space attack success. Neither is a direction ablation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Norm-bounded latent and embedding perturbations partially recover unlearned knowledge.

fits_no_version.finding: Variation in attack success across 65 models lies on a low-dimensional subspace (3 PCs explain 89%). The better of LoRA and full fine-tuning matches or beats the best input-space attack on 64 of 65 models, and on 60 of 65 against a held-out UK AISI attack.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning recovery conservatively bounds prompt-based recovery of unlearned knowledge.

fits_no_version.finding: The activation-rank difference between the base and unlearned models did not correlate with unlearning robustness.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Simple representational-change metrics do not predict unlearning robustness.

fits_no_version.finding: Benign WandA pruning of 15% of weights raises WMDP-Bio on unlearned models only weakly: it beats 20% of input-space attacks, with average relative strength 0.17. It correlates with input-space attack success.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compressing unlearned weights by pruning slightly recovers unlearned knowledge and tracks vulnerability to prompt attacks.

record.code_released: https://huggingface.co/LLM-GAT (models released; code release not stated)
record.problems: Experiments focus on Llama-3-8B-Instruct-derived models. Many per-attack results are shown in figures without corresponding numerical values in the text. The paper does not compare attacked models with a model that never learned the target knowledge, and it reports no explicit chance-level comparison for the claimed recovery results.
record.rows_left_out: Individual attack-by-method values from Figures 2 and 7 and the latent/embedding attack plots are not separately tabulated in the supplied text, so they are not transcribed as numeric rows. The paper also reports correlations and predictive analyses across attacks; these do not directly measure recovery for the claim versions and are not included as rows.

untested.parts: Linear-probe recovery, which the WMDP original used, is not tested.
There is no held-out-fact relearning analysis and no comparison with a model that never learned the knowledge.

There is no activation-direction ablation and no block-vs-delete analysis. The study's internal edits are norm-bounded latent and embedding perturbations, which are not ablations. A brief activation-rank test (null result) is not reported as a recovery result.
There is no quantization attack; quantization appears only as a citation (Zhang et al. 2025). WandA pruning is a different weight edit.
Plain rephrasing and supplying the forgotten facts in context are not tested. Many-shot and translation attacks are reported only in words.

missing.what: Post-unlearning utility (MMLU, MT-Bench, AGIEval) and unlearning score per method, needed to judge A's 'keeps general ability'. For example, GradDiff and TAR have MT-Bench 0.13 and 0.12 and unlearning scores 0.17 and 0.09; the others have MT-Bench 0.68–0.78 and scores 0.73–0.96; the original model has MT-Bench 0.78.

Per-method WMDP-Bio gains for each of the 9 fine-tuning attacks, including which relearning set (forget, retain or WikiText) drives recovery. Benign WikiText fine-tuning (unrelated data) beats 51% of input-space attacks (relative strength 1.72); the best adversarial fine-tuning beats 98% (8.12). Table 4 lists some attack configurations above the text's 16-step, 128-example bound.
Which model-tampering attack gave each method's best tampering score in Table 2. This is needed to link R09–R16 to B.
Per-method gains for each input-space attack (GCG, AutoPrompt, BEAST, PAIR, human prompt).

Summary results: every method gains at least 8 points under its worst-case attack, no model stays below 0.36 after the most effective attack, and every method gains at least 10 points under some fine-tuning attack.

record.verdict_notes:
The record's version IDs V1–V6 were mapped to the declared IDs by what each row measures: V1 (unlearning works / robustness) = A, V2 (fine-tuning recovery) = B, V3 (internal edits) = C, V4 (quantization) = D, V5 (prompting) = E, V6 (counter-methods) = F. Every one of the 21 rows now has a row_fixes item.

Changes from the earlier verdict:
(1) Added the missing row_fixes for R10, R13, R14 and R16 (all A, observed), which the validation required.
(2) Added F to R03 (RMU+LAT, input-space) to match R11.
(3) Added A to R17, R18 and R19, because few-shot fine-tuning is one of the 'simple attacks' in A.
(4) Moved GradDiff and TAR out of the A 'supports' group into a separate A limits_scope group, because neither keeps general ability. The A challenges group now also cites R17 and R18.
(5) Moved R04 out of the F limits_scope group into a new F 'supports' group (RepNoise and RMU+LAT under input attacks, R03 and R04). Its reason notes that non-robust methods resist input attacks about equally.
(6) Flagged a discrepancy inside the paper: the text says fine-tuning used ≤16 steps and ≤128 examples, but Table 4 lists 400-example configurations of 25–50 steps.
(7) Reworked the missing items. Latent and embedding results are no longer listed under E (they fit no version). Added the identity of the best tampering attack per method and the Figure 5 benign fine-tuning numbers.
(8) Added a pruning finding to fits_no_version, and revised the E untested entry, since many-shot is a form of in-context prompting.

Kept from the earlier verdict: input-space gains of 1–2 points are 'absent', not partial, because no uncertainty is reported and such gains are within plausible evaluation noise. The tampering rows R09–R16 stay linked to A rather than B, because Table 2 does not name the winning attack, although the text says fine-tuning was the strongest.

Reading conventions: a row's state describes how much unlearned knowledge came back. Baselines are the unlearned-checkpoint scores; the original model scores 0.70 on WMDP-Bio and chance is 0.25.

Scope limits: RR and ELM carry robustness claims in their own papers, but this text does not present them as robustness methods, so they are not linked to F. Only Llama-3-8B-Instruct derivatives are tested. The jailbreaking experiments measure compliance with harmful requests, not unlearned knowledge, and bear on no version. The study text contains no instructions to the reader.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports WMDP-Bio performance after unlearning and after attacks, but does not establish a chance-level benchmark comparison or compare attacked models with a model that never learned the knowledge.

Fine-tuning attack datasets include WMDP-Bio forget and retain data and WikiText, but the reported text does not give separate recovery results for each dataset or identify which individual facts were relearned.

No activation-direction ablation is reported, and the paper does not analyze whether unlearning blocks access rather than deletes knowledge. It does test latent perturbations, a different internal attack.
No low-bit quantization attack is reported.
The paper tests adversarial input-space attacks and reports unsuccessful many-shot and translation attacks, but does not separately test ordinary rephrasing or other specified prompt-only approaches.
TAR is evaluated against the paper’s attack suite, including fine-tuning attacks. The study does not test every newer counter-method or establish resistance to every attack type.

rows.subject: Llama-3-8B-Instruct + GradDiff best checkpoint
rows.operation_detail: Best input-space attack; WMDP-Bio accuracy after attack
rows.note: Table 2 reports the best input-space attack result for the selected checkpoint; the increase is small.
rows.check: Record says partial. GradDiff goes 0.25→0.27 (+2 points) under the best of 5 input-space attacks, against an original 0.70 and chance 0.25, with no uncertainty reported. That is no recovery beyond plausible noise. GradDiff is dysfluent (MT-Bench 0.13), so it does not meet A's 'keeps general ability' premise.

rows.subject: Utility-preserving state-of-the-art unlearning models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Few-shot fine-tuning attacks to re-elicit WMDP-Bio capability
rows.value: More than 30 percentage points for all utility-preserving state-of-the-art unlearning methods
rows.note: Aggregate statement in the text; individual method-by-attack values are presented as a figure.
rows.check: Aggregate row with no baseline. The relearning sets are WMDP-Bio Remove (the forget corpus), WMDP-Bio Retain (non-hazardous biology, loosely related) and WikiText (unrelated). The text says '16 gradient steps, 128 examples or fewer', but Table 4 lists configurations with 400 examples and 25–50 steps (Full-1, LoRA-1, LoRA-2, Benign-1). A is added because few-shot fine-tuning is a simple attack.

relationships.condition: Best model-tampering attack and few-shot fine-tuning on every method except TAR (GradDiff, RMU, RMU+LAT, RepNoise, ELM, RR, K-FADE)
relationships.reason: Near-chance unlearned scores (0.24–0.32) rise to 0.57–0.71 against an original 0.70 (R09–R14, R16). Utility-preserving methods regain more than 30 points by fine-tuning, and one step adds more than 25 points for 6 of 8 methods (R17, R18).
relationships.display_finding: Attacks raised scores from 0.24–0.32 to 0.57–0.71 against original 0.70; utility-preserving methods regained over 30 points, and one step added over 25 points for six of eight methods.
